groups.high: For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally or is only gasping, activate emergency medical services, obtain an automated external defibrillator (AED) and begin CPR. Follow the dispatcher and AED instructions. American Heart Association guidance recommends chest compressions at 100–120 per minute, at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep while avoiding depths greater than 2.4 inches (6 cm). Position the person on their back on a firm surface. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest on the lower half of the breastbone, with the other hand on top. Keep arms straight and shoulders above the hands. Allow complete chest recoil after every compression without leaning on the chest, and minimise interruptions. An untrained bystander can provide hands-only CPR for a suddenly collapsed adult. A trained, willing rescuer can give cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Continue until professional help takes over, the person shows signs of life, the scene becomes unsafe or you cannot continue.
groups.mid: If an adult will not respond and is not breathing normally, begin the emergency response. Gasping does not count as normal breathing. Call emergency services and get an AED, a device that can give a heart shock. Follow the call handler and the AED's instructions. Put the person on their back on a firm surface. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone. Put your other hand on top. Keep arms straight and shoulders over your hands. Give chest compressions at 100–120 per minute, at least 2 inches, or 5 cm, deep. Avoid going deeper than 2.4 inches, or 6 cm. Allow full chest recoil after each compression without leaning, and keep interruptions short. If you are not trained, use hands-only CPR for a suddenly collapsed adult. If trained and willing, give 30 pushes and 2 breaths. Keep going until help takes over, signs of life return, the place becomes unsafe or you cannot continue.
groups.low: If an adult has collapsed and will not respond, check their breathing. They may not breathe normally, or may only gasp. Call emergency services now and ask for an AED, a device that can shock the heart. Follow its voice and the call handler. Lay the person on their back on a firm surface. Put the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest. Use the lower half of the breastbone. Put your other hand on top. Keep your arms straight with your shoulders above your hands. Push 100–120 times a minute. Push at least 2 inches, or 5 cm, deep. Do not push more than 2.4 inches, or 6 cm. Let the chest rise all the way back without leaning on it, and keep pauses short. Not trained? Use hands-only CPR for an adult who suddenly collapsed. Trained and willing? Give 30 pushes, then 2 breaths. Keep going until help takes over or signs of life return. Stop if the place is unsafe or you cannot go on.
groups.source_review: Checked AHA compression rate/depth, recoil and arrest actions.
groups.notes: Removed false mechanism suggesting complete relaxation should be limited; added emergency activation and AED.

groups.high: Life-threatening external bleeding requires immediate action: call emergency services and apply firm direct pressure using gauze or available clean material. Use gloves or a barrier if available without delaying care. For severe bleeding from an arm or leg, use a manufactured tourniquet according to its instructions if available and you know how. Place it 2–3 inches above the wound, towards the body, never over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops and secure it. Note the application time and tell emergency personnel. Do not loosen or remove it yourself; professional care is urgent. If bleeding continues, follow dispatcher instructions; a second tourniquet placed above the first may be needed. A limb tourniquet is not for the neck, torso, groin or armpit. Use firm direct pressure and, if trained, wound packing for suitable wounds in those areas. Do not remove an embedded object; press around it. Keep the person warm, watch their breathing and remain with them until help arrives.
groups.mid: Heavy bleeding can kill. Call emergency services and press firmly on the wound with gauze or a clean cloth. Use gloves if they are nearby, but do not delay help. For severe bleeding from an arm or leg, use a made-for-purpose tourniquet if you know how. Follow its instructions. Put it 2–3 inches above the wound, towards the body. Do not put it over a joint. Tighten it until the bleeding stops and secure it. Note the time and tell the medical team. Do not loosen or remove it yourself. If bleeding goes on, follow the call handler's advice. A second tourniquet above the first may be needed. Do not use a limb tourniquet on the neck, chest, groin or armpit. Use firm pressure. Pack a suitable wound only if trained. Do not pull out an object stuck in the wound. Press around it. Keep the person warm, watch their breathing and stay until help comes.
groups.low: Life-threatening bleeding needs immediate help, so call emergency services now. Apply firm direct pressure on the wound with gauze or a clean cloth. Use gloves if you have them nearby. Do not delay care to find them. For severe arm or leg bleeding, a tourniquet may help. Use a proper one if you know how. Follow the device guide. Put it 2–3 inches above the wound, towards the body. Never put it over a joint. Tighten it until bleeding stops and secure it in place. Record the time and tell the medical team. Do not loosen or remove it yourself. If blood still flows, ask the call handler what to do. A second one may be needed above the first. Do not put a limb tourniquet on the neck, chest, groin or armpit. Press firmly instead. Pack a suitable wound only if trained. Leave a stuck object in place and press around it. Keep the person warm, watch their breathing and stay until help comes.
groups.source_review: Checked Red Cross direct pressure, tourniquet placement, tightening and trained packing guidance.
groups.notes: Removed dangerous wait-30-minutes assertion, incorrect lower-leg/proximal-knee description and suggestion tourniquet is definitive care.

groups.high: For a thermal burn or scald, stop the burning process safely and cool the affected area under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible. Cooling can still help when started within 3 hours. Remove nearby jewellery and loose clothing before swelling develops, but do not remove material stuck to the skin. Do not apply ice, iced water, butter, toothpaste, creams or ointments during initial first aid. Ice can damage tissue; greasy substances can interfere with cooling and assessment. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children, to avoid whole-body cooling. After cooling, cover loosely with clean non-fluffy material or a layer of cling film; do not wrap tightly around a limb or put cling film on the face. Seek urgent medical help for large or deep burns, burns involving important areas, electrical or chemical burns, or breathing problems. Call emergency services for severe injury. WHO International Health Regulations Annex 7 concerns yellow-fever vaccination, not burn care; this guidance follows NHS burn first aid.
groups.mid: For a burn from heat or hot liquid, move away from the source safely. Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. Start as soon as you can. Cooling may still help within 3 hours. Take off nearby jewellery and loose clothes before swelling starts. Leave anything stuck to the skin in place. Do not use ice, iced water, butter, toothpaste, creams or ointments for first aid. Ice can harm the skin. Greasy things can stop cooling and make the burn harder to check. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially a child. After cooling, cover loosely with a clean cloth that does not shed fluff or a layer of cling film. Do not wrap it tightly round a limb. Do not put cling film on the face. Get urgent care for large or deep burns, burns on important areas, chemical or electrical burns, or breathing trouble. Call emergency services for severe injury. This advice follows NHS burn care. WHO Annex 7 is about yellow-fever vaccines, not burns.
groups.low: Move away from the heat safely. Cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes. Start at once if you can, though cooling can still help within 3 hours. Remove jewellery and loose clothes near the burn, but do not pull off things stuck to the skin. Do not use ice or iced water. Do not put on butter, toothpaste, creams or ointments. Ice can hurt the skin more. Grease can block cooling and make checks hard. Keep the rest of the person warm. Take extra care with a child. Once cool, cover the burn loosely. Use a clean cloth with no fluff, or lay on a sheet of cling film. Do not wrap it tight round a limb. Do not use cling film on the face. Get urgent help for a big or deep burn. Burns on key body areas need care too. So do burns from chemicals or electricity, and breathing trouble. Call emergency services for severe harm. NHS burn advice supports these steps. WHO Annex 7 is about yellow-fever vaccines, not burns.
groups.source_review: Checked NHS cooling, covering and escalation. Corrected erroneous WHO Annex 7 attribution.
groups.notes: Removed invented immediate debridement/hemostasis and mechanistic claims; first aid not surgical care.

groups.high: For severe choking in a responsive adult or child older than 1 year, act when the person cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively. If they can cough forcefully, encourage coughing and monitor instead. Have someone call emergency services while you help. Stand to the side and slightly behind, support the chest and lean the person forward. Give 5 separate firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If the blockage remains, stand behind and give 5 abdominal thrusts: place a fist just above the navel and below the breastbone, grasp it with the other hand, and pull inward and upward. Alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive. Use chest thrusts instead when pregnant or when you cannot reach around the abdomen. If unresponsive, lower them safely and start CPR, following the dispatcher. Remove only an object you can clearly see; never perform blind finger sweeps. Infants under 1 need different care: back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.
groups.mid: If someone can cough strongly, let them cough and watch them. If an adult or child over 1 cannot speak, breathe or cough well, act fast. Ask someone to call emergency services. Stand to the side and just behind. Support their chest and lean them forward. Use the heel of your hand to give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades. If the object stays stuck, give 5 abdominal thrusts. Stand behind and put your fist just above the navel, below the breastbone. Hold the fist with your other hand. Pull in and up. Keep switching between 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive. Use chest thrusts for a pregnant person or if you cannot reach round the belly. If they become unresponsive, lower them safely and start CPR. Follow the call handler. Remove only an object you can see clearly. Never sweep blindly with a finger. For babies under 1, use back blows and chest thrusts, not belly thrusts.
groups.low: If the person can cough strongly, let them cough while you watch. If they cannot speak, breathe or cough well, help now. These steps are for an adult or child over 1. Ask someone to call emergency help. Stand to one side and just behind. Support the chest as you lean them forward. Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If the object is still stuck, stand behind them. Put a fist just above the navel and below the breastbone, holding it with your other hand. Pull in and up 5 times. These are abdominal thrusts. Keep doing 5 back blows, then 5 thrusts. Stop when the object comes out. If they go limp and do not respond, lower them safely. Start CPR and follow the call handler. Use chest thrusts if they are pregnant or you cannot reach round the belly. Do not blindly sweep their mouth. Take out only an object you can see. A baby under 1 needs back blows and chest thrusts, not belly thrusts.
groups.source_review: Checked Mayo first-aid steps, positioning, infants and pregnancy modifications.
groups.notes: Corrected dangerous facing/upright position and false suction explanations; no blind sweep.

groups.high: Use FAST to recognise possible stroke: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty and Time to call emergency services. Ask the person to smile, raise both arms and repeat a simple sentence; one abnormal sign warrants urgent action. Sudden vision loss, severe headache, dizziness or balance trouble can also signal stroke. Call immediately even if symptoms disappear, and note when symptoms began or when the person was last known well. Do not wait to see whether they improve or drive them yourself if emergency transport is available. Do not give food, drink or aspirin unless a clinician instructs you. A clot-blocked artery causes an ischaemic stroke; bleeding causes a haemorrhagic stroke, and treatments differ. Hospital assessment and brain imaging determine eligibility for clot-dissolving drugs. Alteplase, also called tPA, or tenecteplase may be used as soon as possible within 4.5 hours in selected patients; earlier treatment is better. Some patients qualify for other treatments beyond that window. FAST is an emergency recognition tool, not a diagnosis or permission to wait for a treatment deadline.
groups.mid: Use FAST to spot a possible stroke. F means facial drooping: ask the person to smile. A means arm weakness: ask them to raise both arms. S means speech difficulty: ask them to repeat a short sentence. T means time to call emergency medical services. One sign is enough to need emergency assessment. Sudden vision loss, a severe headache or trouble with balance can be symptoms too. Call even if the signs go away. Note when they began, or when the person was last well. Do not wait for things to improve. Use emergency transport if available. Do not give food, drink or aspirin unless a clinician says to. A stroke may be caused by a clot or bleeding, so the hospital needs a brain scan to identify the cause. Some people with a clot can get alteplase, also called tPA, or tenecteplase. These drugs break up clots. They may be given as soon as possible within 4.5 hours in selected patients. Earlier treatment is better. Some other treatments can help later. FAST helps you call for care. It does not diagnose stroke or mean you can wait.
groups.low: FAST helps you recognise a possible stroke. F is for facial drooping. Ask for a smile. A is for arm weakness. Ask them to raise both arms. S is for speech difficulty. Ask for a short sentence. T means time to call emergency medical services. Call for even one of these symptoms. Sudden sight loss, severe headache or loss of balance can matter too. Call even if the signs stop. Record when symptoms began or when the person was last known well. Do not wait or drive them yourself if emergency transport is available. Do not give food, drink or aspirin unless a clinician says to. Stroke can be caused by a clot or bleeding, and a hospital brain scan shows which. Selected patients with a clot may get alteplase, or tPA, or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours. These medicines break up clots. Earlier treatment is better. Other treatment may be possible later. FAST is a warning guide, not a diagnosis. The time limit is not a reason to wait.
groups.source_review: Checked ASA recognition and current thrombolysis window; not individual eligibility advice.
groups.notes: Removed false DAWN/DEFUSE-3 attribution to 4.5-hour tPA window, added tenecteplase and no-wait qualification. Original Mid FK is lower than Low; targeted overlapping allowable ranges without deleting facts.

groups.high: For suspected poison ingestion, seek substance-specific advice immediately rather than waiting for symptoms. Call emergency services if the person collapses, has a seizure, cannot be awakened or has breathing difficulty. Otherwise contact your local poison service; in the United States, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. Do not induce vomiting or give ipecac. Vomiting can cause choking or expose the throat to a corrosive substance again. Do not improvise treatments, force drinks or give anything by mouth to someone who is drowsy, convulsing or unable to swallow safely. The appropriate advice depends on the substance; some caustic exposures have specific dilution advice from Poison Control. Keep the container and report the product, strength, estimated amount, time swallowed, age, weight and symptoms. Do not delay the call while trying to obtain exact quantities. Follow professional instructions about observation, emergency assessment or treatment. Antidotes and decontamination are clinical decisions, not general home remedies.
groups.mid: If someone may have swallowed poison, get advice now. Do not wait for symptoms. If they collapse, have a seizure, cannot wake up or struggle to breathe, call emergency services. Otherwise call a local poison service. In the United States, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. Do not make them vomit or give ipecac. Vomit can cause choking or burn the throat again. Do not try a home cure or force them to drink. Give nothing by mouth if they are drowsy, having a seizure or cannot swallow safely. What to do depends on the poison. Poison Control may advise a small drink for some burning substances, but this is not a rule for all poisons. Keep the packet or bottle. Say what was swallowed, its strength, how much and when. Give the person's age, weight and symptoms if known. Call even if the amount is not clear. Follow advice about hospital care or watching for symptoms. Antidotes and other treatments need a professional decision.
groups.low: Someone may have swallowed poison. Get advice now. Do not wait for signs of illness. Call emergency help if they collapse, have a seizure or cannot wake up. Call if they cannot breathe well too. If not, call your local poison service. In the US, call Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. Do not make them throw up. Do not give ipecac. Vomit may choke them or burn the throat again. Do not try a home cure. Do not force a drink. Give nothing by mouth if they are sleepy, having a seizure or cannot swallow safely. Advice depends on the poison. Some burning poisons may need a small drink, but only follow expert advice. Keep the bottle or packet. Say what it was and how strong it was. Say how much was taken and when, if known. Give the person's age, weight and signs of illness. Do not delay the call to find exact amounts. Follow the expert's advice. Special treatments are not home cures.
groups.source_review: Checked Poison Control emergency escalation, no vomiting and substance-specific advice.
groups.notes: Removed demand for exact dose before contact and substituted safe, non-delaying identification advice.

groups.high: For low blood glucose in a person who is awake and can swallow safely, the American Diabetes Association describes the 15–15 rule: take 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes and recheck. A reading below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) usually requires treatment; follow the person's diabetes plan. If it remains below 70 mg/dL, repeat 15 grams and recheck after another 15 minutes. Examples include half a cup, or 4 ounces, of juice or regular non-diet soda, or glucose tablets or gel providing 15 grams according to the label. Tablet size varies; four 4-gram tablets contain 16 grams, not exactly 15. Fat or fibre can slow absorption, so chocolate is not a first choice. Once recovered, take a carbohydrate-and-protein snack if the next meal is not soon. Never give food or drink to someone unconscious, having a seizure or unable to swallow. Use prescribed glucagon if available and trained to do so, and obtain emergency help. Children and some automated insulin-delivery users may need a different amount under their care plan. Severe hypoglycaemia is defined by the need for help, not a single glucose number or the imprecise term diabetic shock.
groups.mid: The American Diabetes Association recommends the 15–15 rule for low blood glucose in someone who is awake and able to swallow safely. Blood glucose is the medical term for blood sugar. A measurement below 70 mg/dL, or 3.9 mmol/L, usually requires treatment according to the person's individual diabetes plan. Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes and recheck the reading. If it is still below 70 mg/dL, repeat the treatment and check again after 15 minutes. Suitable choices include half a cup, or 4 ounces, of juice or regular non-diet soda. Glucose tablets or gel are alternatives; check the label for the amount providing 15 grams. Four tablets with 4 grams each give 16 grams, not 15. Fat and fibre slow absorption, so chocolate is not the first choice. After recovery, offer a snack with carbohydrate and protein if the next meal is not soon. Never give food or drink if the person is unconscious, having a seizure or unable to swallow. Administer prescribed glucagon if available and you are trained, and obtain emergency medical assistance. Children and some insulin-pump users need a different amount under their care plan. Severe low glucose means the person needs help, not just one fixed reading.
groups.low: Hypoglycaemia means low blood glucose, or low blood sugar. If the person is awake and can swallow safely, use their diabetes plan. The American Diabetes Association gives a 15–15 rule. A reading below 70 mg/dL, or 3.9 mmol/L, usually needs treatment. Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes and check the glucose again. If it is still below 70 mg/dL, give another 15 grams. Recheck after 15 minutes. Half a cup, or 4 ounces, of juice or regular soda can work. Do not use diet soda. Glucose tablets or gel are alternatives; check the label for the amount providing 15 grams. Four 4-gram tablets give 16 grams, not 15. Fat and fibre slow absorption, so chocolate is not the first choice. Once better, have a snack with carbohydrate and protein if a meal is not soon. Never give food or drink to a person who is unconscious, has a seizure or cannot swallow. Give prescribed glucagon if you have it and know how. Get emergency help. Children and some insulin-pump users need a different amount in their care plan. Severe low sugar means needing help, not just one fixed reading.
groups.source_review: Checked ADA 15–15, amounts, repeat threshold, snack and severe hypoglycaemia safeguards.
groups.notes: Corrected dangerous 30–45 mL juice dose, incorrect rejection of regular soda, 4x4g arithmetic, conscious/severe definitions and fixed-dose universalism.

groups.high: Suspected heat stroke is a medical emergency. Confusion, collapse, seizures or other altered mental function after heat exposure require emergency help and immediate cooling. Do not wait for a temperature reading or for sweating to stop. Move the person to shade or a cooler place and remove excess clothing. Cool or cold-water immersion, including an ice bath where feasible, provides rapid cooling; support the person's head and airway continuously and never leave them unattended in water. If immersion is unavailable, soak the skin or clothing, apply cool wet towels and fan vigorously. Cold packs at the neck, armpits and groin can supplement cooling. Do not force fluids, especially if confused or unable to swallow. Keep cooling while emergency help is arranged. Trained responders may monitor core temperature and stop active cooling around 101–102°F (38.3–38.9°C) to prevent overcooling; do not delay first aid to measure it. Continued medical assessment is necessary even after apparent recovery. Do not give sedatives or other medicines as home treatment.
groups.mid: Heat stroke is a life-threatening condition requiring emergency medical care. Confusion, collapse or a seizure after heat exposure can be warning signs. Call emergency services and start cooling at once. Do not wait for a temperature measurement or assume that sweating excludes heat stroke. Move them into shade or a cool place and remove extra clothes. Cool or cold water immersion can cool fast; an ice bath can work if safe and practical. Maintain support for the head and airway, and never leave the person unattended in water. If there is no bath, wet the skin or clothes with cool water. Use wet towels and fan hard. Cold packs at the neck, armpits and groin can help too. Do not force drinks, especially if they are confused or cannot swallow. Keep cooling while help is arranged. Trained responders may check core temperature and stop active cooling around 101–102°F, or 38.3–38.9°C, to avoid overcooling. Do not delay care to take a reading. They still need medical checks even if they seem better. Do not administer sedatives or other medicines as home treatment.
groups.low: Heat stroke is a medical emergency. Confusion, collapse or a seizure after heat exposure can be warning signs. Call emergency services and begin immediate cooling. Do not wait for a heat reading. They may still sweat. Move them to shade or a cool place. Take off extra clothes. A bath of cool or cold water can cool them fast. An ice bath can help if safe to use. Support the head and airway, and never leave the person unattended in water. If no bath is available, soak the skin or clothing. Put on cool wet towels and fan them hard. Cold packs on the neck, armpits and groin can help. Do not force fluids, especially if they are confused or unable to swallow safely. Keep cooling as help is called. Trained staff may check core temperature. They may stop active cooling at 101–102°F, or 38.3–38.9°C, to stop overcooling. Do not delay care to check it yourself. Medical assessment is still needed even after apparent recovery. Do not give sedatives or home medicines.
groups.source_review: Checked CDC cooling and emergency response; approximate stopping range is for monitored responders, not delay criterion.
groups.notes: Removed unsupported cooling rate and dangerous lay sedative instructions; corrected blanket exclusion of ice-cold cooling.

groups.high: Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening allergic reaction requiring prompt intramuscular epinephrine and emergency medical help. Use the person's prescribed auto-injector according to its own instructions. For EpiPen or EpiPen Jr, remove the blue safety release, keep fingers away from both ends, place the orange tip against the middle of the outer thigh and press firmly until it activates. It can be used through clothing if necessary. Hold in place for 3 seconds, remove it, then massage the site for 10 seconds as the manufacturer directs. Hold a child's thigh firmly to prevent movement. Do not inject into the buttock, hands, feet or a vein. Call emergency services immediately; symptoms can recur and further care may be necessary. A second device may be needed if symptoms continue or return; follow the emergency plan and professional advice. EpiPen delivers 0.3 mg for people weighing at least 30 kg; EpiPen Jr delivers 0.15 mg for 15–30 kg. Other brands and weight groups have different instructions. Do not delay emergency epinephrine because of a cardiac condition; obtain professional help.
groups.mid: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction. Use the person's prescribed epinephrine auto-injector at once and call emergency help. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for that specific device. For EpiPen or EpiPen Jr, take off the blue safety release. Keep fingers away from both ends. Put the orange tip on the middle of the outer thigh and press firmly until it works. It can go through clothing if needed. Hold it there for 3 seconds. Take it away and massage the spot for 10 seconds, as the maker says. Hold a child's thigh still so they do not move. Do not inject into hands, feet, buttocks or a vein. Get emergency care even if they seem better, since symptoms can return. A second device may be needed if symptoms stay or return. Follow the emergency plan and professional advice. EpiPen gives 0.3 mg for people at least 30 kg. EpiPen Jr gives 0.15 mg for 15–30 kg. Other brands or weights need their own directions. Do not delay this emergency drug due to a heart condition.
groups.low: A severe allergy can kill. It is called anaphylaxis. Use the person's prescribed epinephrine pen now. Call emergency help too. Read the guide for that pen. For EpiPen or EpiPen Jr, pull off the blue safety release. Keep fingers off both ends. Put the orange tip on the middle of the outer thigh. Press firmly until it works. It can go through clothes if needed. Hold for 3 seconds. Take it away. Massage the spot for 10 seconds, as the maker says. Hold a child's leg still. Do not inject into the hands, feet, buttocks or a vein. Get emergency care even if they feel better. Signs can come back. A second pen may be needed if signs stay or return. Follow the emergency plan and expert advice. EpiPen gives 0.3 mg for a person at least 30 kg. EpiPen Jr gives 0.15 mg for 15–30 kg. Other pens and weights have their own guides. A heart problem is not a reason to delay the emergency drug.
groups.source_review: Checked manufacturer EpiPen instructions, site, 3-second hold, 10-second massage and device-specific dosing.
groups.notes: Corrected harmful instruction to allow bleeding/avoid site pressure, and made three-second hold brand-specific.

groups.high: During a seizure, stay with the person, time the event and protect them from injury. Clear nearby hazards, cushion the head and loosen tight clothing around the neck. Do not restrain movements or put anything in the mouth. Turn the person gently onto their side when possible to help keep the airway clear, and remain until they are alert and recovering. Do not offer food, drink or pills until fully awake and able to swallow. Follow an available seizure action plan, including prescribed rescue medication only if authorised and trained. Call emergency services for a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, repeated seizures without recovery, a first seizure, serious injury, breathing difficulty or failure to return to the usual state. A seizure in water also needs emergency help. If breathing does not resume after movements stop, follow dispatcher instructions and start CPR if needed. Do not wait for a 30-minute threshold when seizures repeat or recovery is poor. A prolonged convulsive seizure can be status epilepticus and requires urgent treatment.
groups.mid: Stay with a person having a seizure and note the time it starts. Move hard or sharp things away. Cushion the head and loosen tight clothes round the neck. Do not hold them down or put anything in the mouth. Turn them gently onto their side when you can, so the airway stays clear. Stay until they are alert and recovering. Give no food, drink or pills until they are fully awake and can swallow. Follow their seizure action plan if one is available. Give prescribed rescue medicine only if trained and authorised. Call emergency services if the seizure lasts 5 minutes or more. Call for repeated seizures without recovery, a first seizure, serious injury, trouble breathing or failure to return to their usual state. A seizure in water also needs emergency help. If they do not breathe after shaking stops, follow the call handler and start CPR if needed. Do not wait 30 minutes for repeat seizures or poor recovery. A long seizure can become status epilepticus, a medical emergency.
groups.low: Stay with the person and time the seizure. Move sharp and hard things away. Put something soft under the head. Loosen tight clothes at the neck. Do not hold them down. Do not put anything in the mouth. Turn them gently onto their side when you can. This helps keep the airway clear. Stay until they are alert and recovering. Give no food, drink or pills until they are fully awake and can swallow. Follow a seizure action plan if they have one. Give prescribed rescue medicine only if trained and allowed to do so. Call emergency services at 5 minutes or more. Call if seizures repeat without recovery. Call for a first seizure, a bad injury, breathing trouble or poor recovery too. A seizure in water needs emergency help. If breathing does not start after shaking stops, follow the call handler. Start CPR if needed. Do not wait 30 minutes for repeat seizures or poor recovery. A long seizure may be status epilepticus. That needs urgent medical care.
groups.source_review: Checked Epilepsy Foundation seizure first aid and escalation criteria.
groups.notes: Removed 30-minute delay criterion and overly narrow tertiary-centre/diagnostic claims; included do-not-restrain/do-not-mouth safeguards.
